about: Most link-safety checkers work by fetching the URL from a server, which means the scanner itself visits the suspicious site, tips off the attacker and can be fooled by pages that behave differently for bots. Link Checker takes the opposite route: it never requests the page. It reads the URL string itself, because the string already contains most of the clues that separate a phishing link from a legitimate one: look-alike characters, a misleading hostname, a redirect hidden in a query parameter, a risky file name or a secret in the query string.

It is useful for people who triage reports of suspicious email, for support and security staff who forward links to colleagues, and for anyone who wants to clean tracking parameters out of a URL before sharing it. Paste up to 30 links, one per line (each up to 2,000 characters), and every link gets a list of findings ranked as high, warning or info, plus a decoded chain of any hidden destinations.

There is one optional network step. A dig-style DNS lookup is sent through the Trick-it host's `dns-query` permission, and the browser asks public DNS-over-HTTPS resolvers (Cloudflare, Google and Cloudflare's malware-filtering resolver) for A, AAAA, CNAME, NS, MX and CAA records. Only the hostname goes to those resolvers; the site itself is never contacted, and you can skip the lookup entirely.

features.title: Spoofing and lookalike detection
features.body: Flags mixed scripts, Unicode confusables, Punycode/IDN hosts, control and bidirectional characters, `user@host` userinfo tricks, encoded delimiters and unusual ports, all of which are ways to make one hostname look like another.

features.title: Hidden destination decoding
features.body: Unwraps redirects embedded in the URL: nested URL parameters (including base64), Microsoft Safe Links, Proofpoint v2 and v3, Google `/url`, Facebook `l.php` and outbound wrappers from YouTube, LinkedIn, Slack and Reddit. Known URL shorteners are flagged, since their target cannot be known without visiting them.

features.title: Brand impersonation heuristics
features.body: Compares hostnames with a bounded list of brands and their official domains, catching one-character edits such as `paypa1.com`, brand names used as subdomains of another domain, and login or verification words on unrelated hosts.

features.title: Dig-style DNS lookup
features.body: Shows all returned records in a sortable table and detects non-existent domains, private or rebinding answers, domains blocked by the malware-filtering resolver, dangling CNAMEs pointing at takeover-prone services, resolver disagreement, fast-flux style TTLs and DNSSEC validation.

features.title: Share-safe cleanup
features.body: Removes tracking parameters (utm_*, fbclid, gclid, msclkid and similar) and secret-looking parameters such as tokens, keys, sessions and signatures, so a link you forward does not carry your identity.

features.title: Command and report export
features.body: Because a browser cannot read cross-origin redirect chains, the tool generates shell-safe `curl` and `dig` commands to run yourself, plus a downloadable JSON report of the findings.

reference.title: What the checks look at and how to read them

blocks.text: A URL is split into scheme, userinfo, host, port, path, query and fragment, and attackers abuse each part differently. Only the host decides where the browser connects, yet people read left to right and trust whatever comes first.

head: Pattern
Why it is suspicious
Example
rows: Everything before `@` is a username, so the real host is after it
The registrable domain is the last labels, not the first
The ASCII form of an internationalised name; may hide lookalikes
Decimal, hex or octal forms of an address skip name-based filters
The visible name suggests a document while the real type is executable
Cheap TLDs are over-represented in abuse; `.zip` and `.mov` also resemble file names

blocks.text: Targets that point at private, loopback, link-local or cloud-metadata addresses, and names such as `localhost` or `.internal`, are marked high. They matter for server-side request forgery rather than phishing: a link that makes a backend fetch `169.254.169.254` is an attack on the backend.

items: High: strong indicators such as confusable characters, mixed scripts, misleading userinfo, brand impersonation, double extensions, HTTP login pages, private targets, dangling CNAMEs or a domain blocked by the malware-filter resolver.

Warning: signals that often accompany abuse but have legitimate uses: URL shorteners, redirect wrappers, Punycode, unusual ports, abused TLDs, secret-looking parameters, very long URLs, DNS that does not resolve.
Info: facts worth knowing: tracking hosts, archives, `blob:` URLs, a clean DNS result, DNSSEC status.

blocks.text: No warnings does not mean safe. The checks are heuristics, the confusable table is bounded rather than a full UTS #39 implementation, and a brand-new phishing domain on a normal TLD can pass every check.

DNS over HTTPS (RFC 8484) lets a browser ask a resolver a DNS question as an HTTPS request. The tool asks more than one resolver and compares them. A NXDOMAIN answer means the name does not exist, which usually means a typo or an expired phishing domain. If the malware-filtering resolver returns no answer while a standard resolver does, the domain is flagged as blocked.

A dangling CNAME is a record that points to a hosting service such as GitHub Pages, Heroku, Azure or S3 where the target account no longer exists, which allows someone else to claim it and serve content on the original name. The tool matches CNAME targets against a list of such suffixes. Private answers (for example a public name resolving to `10.x.x.x`) indicate DNS rebinding or a misconfiguration. A TTL of 60 seconds or less combined with four or more addresses is reported as fast-flux style.

sections.heading: Commands for the checks a browser cannot do

blocks.text: To follow redirects yourself without a browser, run the generated `curl` command, which asks only for headers. Run it from an isolated machine if you are triaging a hostile link, and compare the final `Location` with the decoded chain.
An email claims an unpaid invoice and links to the address below. Paste it into the checker and read the results from the top.

items: The wrapper is decoded, so the hidden chain shows `secure-paypa1.top` as the real destination instead of the security-vendor hostname.
High findings appear for brand impersonation (`paypa1` is one character away from `paypal`) and the double extension `.pdf.exe`.
Warnings appear for the abused `.top` TLD and the secret-looking `token` parameter.

Run the DNS lookup. If the name returns no records or the malware resolver blocks it, the result confirms it. Then use the share-safe cleanup if you need to forward a sanitised copy to the security team.

limits: It cannot say a link is safe. Heuristics produce false positives for legitimate shorteners and brand mentions and false negatives for new, well-formed phishing domains.
Live redirect chains are not followed. A shortener's final destination is unknown until you run the generated `curl` command or use a dedicated expander in a sandbox.
The page content, certificates and domain age are never inspected, since the site is never visited.
Each run is limited to 30 links of at most 2,000 characters, and the brand and confusable lists are finite.
DNS lookups need the host's `dns-query` permission and network access to the public resolvers, so the DNS step does not work offline.

faq.question: Does Link Checker open the link I paste?
faq.answer: No. The analysis is done on the text of the URL. The optional DNS lookup contacts public resolvers, not the website itself.

faq.question: What is sent during a DNS lookup?
faq.answer: Only the hostname and the record type, to the Cloudflare and Google DNS-over-HTTPS resolvers and Cloudflare's malware-filtering resolver, through the host's `dns-query` broker. The path and query of your URL stay local.

faq.question: Why does a shortened link only show a warning?
faq.answer: A shortener hides its destination behind a server-side redirect, which cannot be read without making a request. The tool flags it and gives you a `curl` command to inspect the redirect safely.

faq.question: Why was my legitimate link flagged?
faq.answer: Findings are signals, not verdicts. Tracking wrappers, shorteners, ports and long query strings are common in genuine marketing email. Check the high-level findings first and the hostname second.

faq.question: Which parameters does the cleanup remove?
faq.answer: Tracking parameters such as utm_*, fbclid, gclid, msclkid and mc_eid, and secret-looking ones such as token, api_key, password, session, signature and otp.

faq.question: Can I check a link's DNS records like the dig command?
faq.answer: Yes. The lookup table lists A, AAAA, CNAME, NS, MX and CAA records from each resolver. For other tools that use hostnames, see [Encoder Decoder](/encoder-decoder/) to decode URL-encoded or base64 parameters by hand.
